prompt:
# Write one principle card

You are writing a **principle card**: one mechanism, stated so precisely that
somebody who has never seen your sources could implement it and somebody else
could prove it wrong.

The card is not the implementation. A later step turns it into a behaviour-tree
leaf, and that step will be given **your card and nothing else** — not this
prompt, not your reasoning, not whatever you were given below. So everything the
implementer needs has to survive inside the six fields.

## The system the principle has to fit

A Unitree Go2 quadruped navigating an indoor space it has no map of. Below the
behaviour tree sits an inherited, pretrained, **frozen** locomotion policy: the
only thing anything ever sends the robot is a Twist — `(vx, vy, wz)`, saturated
to `|vx|, |vy| <= 0.8 m/s` and `|wz| <= 1.0 rad/s`. Nothing you write touches the
policy, the gait or the joints.

What the robot can sense, once per control step:

```
t                    sim seconds since the episode started
ranges               181 lidar beams over a full circle, metres, inf where no return
range_angles         beam bearings in the ROBOT frame, radians
range_max            6.0 — what "as far as I can see" means
pose_estimate        (x, y, yaw) — the BELIEF about our pose, never ground truth
pose_error_estimate  scalar metres — how wrong we believe that belief is
contact              bool — are we touching something right now
goal                 (x, y), or None meaning NOT DISCLOSED
```

Two of those are traps. `pose_estimate` **drifts** on some scenarios — a seeded
random walk is added to it — and ground truth is never observable. `goal` may be
`None`, meaning the goal exists and the episode is still scored against it but
this robot has not found it yet; it latches once seen.

## The task family this principle has to be useful for

Reach a goal whose position is NOT disclosed. `obs.goal` is None until the robot has been close enough to see the goal with nothing in the way, after which it latches. Until then the task is to cover ground that has not been covered, in an indoor space with no map.

<!-- ---- SOURCE BLOCK BEGIN ---- -->
## What to base the principle on

The full text of a published paper is reproduced below. Read it and extract the
principle it establishes.

```
[PAPER TEXT REDACTED FROM THIS TRANSCRIPT — 73099 characters, sha256(pdf)=ff51f04ec7e6c174, extractor=cache. The corpus is an input and is never committed (out/corpus/ is gitignored). The prompt_hash recorded beside this is the hash of the REAL prompt, so a machine holding the PDF re-renders it byte-identically and replay finds this transcript.]
```

Work from the document, not from your memory of it. Where the two disagree, the
document wins. Quote its own threshold, exponent or closed form where it states
one, and put the section, page or equation number in `span` so somebody else can
check it.

The paper was written about something other than a quadruped with a planar
lidar. Carrying it across is the `derivation` field's whole job: say what in the
original maps onto what here, and say plainly where the mapping is yours rather
than the paper's.
<!-- ---- SOURCE BLOCK END ---- -->

## What a card is

Six fields. `mechanism`, `trigger` and `derivation` are prose. `prediction` is
**structured**, because a prediction that cannot be decided automatically cannot
become a unit test — and this one will be run as one, with no human in the loop.

```yaml
id: <short_snake_case_identifier>
node_name: <TheLeafThisWouldProduce>       # CamelCase, verb-first

source:
  citation: <the reference this principle comes from, or the single line
             "(no source - the principle was devised, not extracted)" if it
             comes from none>
  span: <the section, page, figure or equation number where the mechanism is
         stated — the part that makes a threshold checkable. LEAVE EMPTY if you
         cannot point at a location you are sure of.>

mechanism: <what happens, and why it helps. The finding, not the implementation.>
trigger: <the condition under which it applies -> becomes the precondition port>
derivation: <how that becomes a rule for THIS robot and THESE sensors. Numbers
             belong here, with their units, and so does the reasoning that got
             you to them.>

prediction:
  statement: <the falsifiable claim, in words>
  metric: <what gets better>
  baseline: <goal_seeker or reactive_avoid>
  min_effect: <a number: the smallest effect that would count as support>
  cost_metric: <the metric this mechanism is expected to make WORSE>

confidence: <high | medium | low>
```

### `prediction.metric` — the closed list

The metric must be one the scorer actually computes, and one a **controller can
move**. These and no others:

| metric | better |
|---|---|
| `goal_reached` | higher (a rate over seeds) |
| `spl` | higher (path efficiency) |
| `min_clearance` | higher (closest approach to anything, metres) |
| `collisions`, `near_misses` | lower |
| `stuck_events`, `time_stuck`, `recovery_time` | lower |
| `time_to_goal`, `path_length` | lower |

`localisation_failures`, `optimal_distance`, `scenario` and `seed` are **not
available**: no controller can move them, so a prediction naming one is not
falsifiable about the node and the card is rejected at load.

`cost_metric` is the honest counterpart — the metric this mechanism is expected
to make worse. A mechanism that buys clearance with time should say so. It may
be empty only if you genuinely believe the mechanism costs nothing, and you
should be suspicious of that belief.

### `confidence` — criteria about the SOURCE, not about how sure you feel

- **high** — the mechanism *and* its quantitative form are stated explicitly in
  a source you can point at; the span points at the equation, threshold or
  exponent itself.
- **medium** — the mechanism is stated explicitly somewhere, but the
  quantitative form is adapted: different units, a different body scale, a
  different sensor. The number is yours; the mechanism is not.
- **low** — the mechanism is qualitative and the derivation is entirely yours.
  Still usable, but it is your claim, and the card must not read otherwise.

## Rules

- **One mechanism.** A card describing two is two cards. This is not a style
  rule: the unit scenario that decides admissibility has to isolate one claimed
  effect, and it cannot isolate two.
- **No coupling to a specific scenario.** The leaf will run on worlds nobody has
  seen. The card may not name a room, a coordinate, a doorway or a map.
- **Do not invent a `span`.** An empty span is a result and costs nothing. A
  section number reconstructed from the shape of such papers is a fabrication,
  it will be checked against the document, and it is the single failure this
  pipeline exists to detect.
- **Do not invent numbers.** If a source states a threshold, an exponent or a
  closed form, give it and say where. If it does not, derive one, say the
  derivation is yours, and set `confidence: low`.

## What to return

One fenced ```yaml block containing exactly one card, and nothing else that
looks like YAML. Prose outside the fence — including, if it applies, an honest
statement of what you did not know.

response.text:
```yaml
id: geometric_shape_revisit_reroute
node_name: RerouteAtShapeRecognisedPlace

source:
  citation: >
    Cheng, K. (1986). A purely geometric module in the rat's spatial
    representation. Cognition, 23, 149-178.
  span: >
    General Discussion, pp. 171-172 (the displacement-properties argument and
    the "A geometric module" section, which opens on p. 172): "the rat must have
    recorded the metric relations of distances and angles between target and
    shape, and kept track of left-right relations, or sense... That rats do not
    systematically make affine or reflection errors at quadrants adjacent to the
    correct one, but do make rotational errors, indicates that they encode and
    use both metric relations and sense". Quantitative anchors: Exp. 1A
    Discussion, p. 158 ("The 3 : 2 ratio of correct digs to rotational errors
    means, however, that the animals were only 20% above chance at
    distinguishing the correct location from the rotational error"); Exp. 1A
    Apparatus p. 153 ("a wooden box (120 X 60 cm)") and Results p. 157 ("If a dig
    was within 15 cm of the centre of the food dish, it was correct... A circle
    of 15 cm radius covers 10% of the surface area"); Exp. 3 Discussion p. 170
    (transposition of features costs nothing, affine/reflection of geometry
    costs performance).

mechanism: >
  A place can be identified by the SHAPE of the surrounding surfaces alone -
  "the arrangement of surfaces as surfaces" - held as a record specified by
  displacement properties: metric distances and angles PLUS sense (handedness).
  Cheng's rats matched such a record to the world rigidly and non-mirrored. The
  evidence is the error signature: in a rectangle their mistakes were almost
  exclusively at the location 180 degrees rotated through the centre (Exp. 1A,
  Table 1, p. 158: 47% correct, 31% rotational, 22% other), which is exactly the
  second rigid congruence a rectangle admits, and there were no reflection or
  affine errors at the adjacent quadrants, which are the congruences the record
  would admit if sense or metric were dropped (pp. 171-172). Why shape-keyed
  identity helps: it is invariant to everything except geometry. Rearranging all
  the surface features while leaving geometry intact (the diagonal transposition,
  Exp. 3) cost the rats nothing; changing the geometric relations while keeping
  the local feature (affine transformation or reflection) made every rat's
  performance drop (p. 170). And it never consults the animal's belief about
  where it is. The price is precisely one failure mode, and the paper measures
  it: when the shape is self-congruent under rotation the record cannot pick
  between the two fits, and the rats were "only 20% above chance" at doing so
  (p. 158). So a shape record is a trustworthy place key exactly when its own
  best fit is decisively better than its next rotational fit, and a detector
  built on it must refuse to answer when it is not.

trigger: >
  obs.goal is None (goal not yet disclosed, so the task is covering unvisited
  ground); the current scan has at least 30 finite returns (enough structure to
  constitute a shape); and the shape memory holds at least one record captured
  more than 4.0 m of accumulated commanded travel ago. If any of these fails,
  the node returns FAILURE on the same tick and the tree falls through to
  whatever explorer sits below it.

derivation: >
  MAPPING. "Arrangement of surfaces as surfaces" -> the 181-beam range profile,
  inf replaced by range_max = 6.0 m, which is a featureless record of where
  surfaces are and nothing about what they look like. "Metric relations" -> the
  range values in metres. "Sense" -> the beam ORDER around the circle. "Rigid
  congruence of record to world" -> circular shift of the profile, because
  range_angles are robot-frame, so a yaw change is exactly a circular shift.
  "Rotational error" -> a shift other than the true one that fits nearly as well.
  The rat's non-geometric features (brightness, odour) have no analogue on this
  sensor and are simply absent; that absence is the paper's point, not a loss.
  The paper is about returning to a remembered goal; using the same record to
  detect that you are somewhere you have already been, and to leave by a
  different exit, is MY extension, not Cheng's.

  DESCRIPTOR. r[i] = min(ranges[i], 6.0) for the N distinct bearings (N = 181;
  if range_angles wraps so the last beam duplicates the first, drop it and use
  N = 180). Beam pitch d_ang = 2*pi/N rad (about 1.99 deg).

  MATCH. For shift k in [0, N): d(k) = (1/N) * sum_i |r_cur[i] - r_rec[(i+k) mod
  N]|, in metres. d* = min_k d(k), k* = argmin. NEVER evaluate the mirrored
  comparison (r_rec reversed): rats make no reflection errors, so sense is part
  of the record (pp. 171-172). This is the paper's constraint, carried over
  unchanged.

  ACCEPT. Declare a revisit iff d* <= tau, with tau = clip(0.125 * m, 0.20,
  0.75) metres, where m is the median finite range of the stored record. The
  0.125 is the rats' scoring tolerance expressed as a fraction of their arena:
  15 cm radius in a 120 cm box (pp. 153, 157). Reading that ratio as a
  scale-relative match tolerance and applying it in range-difference space is
  MINE; the clip bounds (0.20 m, 0.75 m) are mine, set so a tight corridor does
  not demand sub-decimetre agreement and a large open room does not accept
  everything.

  REFUSE WHEN AMBIGUOUS. Let k2 = argmin d(k) over shifts whose circular
  separation from k* is at least 23 beams (about 45 deg). If d(k2) <= 1.20 * d*,
  the shape is rotationally self-similar - a corridor, a square room, a bare
  rectangle - and the node returns FAILURE without acting and without writing an
  exit. The 1.20 is the rats' own margin: a 3:2 correct-to-rotational split is
  "only 20% above chance" (p. 158), i.e. 20% is the observed level at which two
  rigid fits remain confusable. Transplanting that percentage into descriptor-
  score space is MINE.

  ACT. Each record stores, besides r, the set E of exit bearings in ITS OWN
  frame: the mean commanded motion bearing atan2(vy, vx) over the 1.0 m of
  travel following capture. On an accepted, unambiguous match, k* converts them
  into the current robot frame: phi_cur = wrap(phi_rec - k* * d_ang), with the
  sign following the indexing above (implementers must keep the convention
  consistent with their correlation). Choose the target bearing theta* that
  maximises the minimum circular distance to every phi_cur, subject to (a)
  min(r) over beams within +/-20 deg of theta* being >= 1.2 m, and (b) that
  minimum circular distance being >= 60 deg (1.05 rad). If no bearing satisfies
  both, return FAILURE. Otherwise command vy = 0, wz = clip(1.5 * wrap(theta* -
  0), -1.0, 1.0) with the error measured against the robot's own forward axis,
  and vx = 0.5 m/s once |error| <= 0.35 rad, else vx = 0. Hold RUNNING until the
  robot has covered 1.0 m along the new exit, then append that exit to the
  record's E and return SUCCESS. 4.0 m blackout, 1.2 m corridor width, 60 deg
  exit separation, the 1.5 gain and the 0.5 m/s crawl are all MINE: the blackout
  keeps consecutive frames in a corridor from matching themselves, 1.2 m clears a
  Go2 plus margin, 60 deg is a heading change larger than the descriptor's own
  ambiguity window.

  POSE. pose_estimate is never read by this node. Place identity comes only from
  the scan; the only integrated quantity is commanded-travel distance, used as a
  monotone counter for the blackout, where drift in its absolute value is
  harmless.

prediction:
  statement: >
    On scenarios where obs.goal is None at episode start, inserting this leaf
    above the default explorer raises the fraction of seeds on which the goal is
    found, because shape-keyed revisit detection breaks the loop-and-re-tread
    behaviour that pose-keyed or pose-free exploration falls into once
    pose_estimate has drifted. It is falsified if goal_reached fails to improve
    by the stated margin, and the mechanism specifically (rather than the extra
    turning) is falsified if allowing the mirrored match or deleting the 1.20
    ambiguity guard leaves goal_reached unchanged.
  metric: goal_reached
  baseline: reactive_avoid
  min_effect: 0.10
  cost_metric: path_length

confidence: medium
```

What I am not claiming. The paper never says a word about revisit detection, exploration, or leaving a place by an unused exit — Cheng's rats were returning to a remembered goal, not avoiding covered ground. The invariance result (shape-keyed identity survives a total feature rearrangement, fails under geometric change) and the error signature (rotational errors only, never reflection or affine) are his; the decision to use that same record as a *coverage* key is mine, and it is the load-bearing leap in the card.

Two of the three numbers are transplants rather than measurements. `0.125` is the rats' 15 cm scoring radius divided by their 120 cm box, reinterpreted as a scale-relative tolerance on mean range difference — a different space entirely, and nothing in the paper licenses that. `1.20` is the paper's own "20% above chance" (p. 158), which describes how well rats discriminated two fits, reused as a required score margin between two fits; again my move. Only the exclusion of mirrored matching is the paper's number-free constraint carried straight across. Hence `medium`, not `high`.

One thing I could not resolve from the document: whether 181 beams over "a full circle" means 180 intervals of exactly 2° with the endpoints distinct or the first bearing repeated at the end. The card handles both by dropping a duplicate bearing before correlating, but a wrong choice here rotates every alignment by one beam (~2°), which is well inside the 45° ambiguity window and so does not change the accept/refuse decision.
